newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN APRIL CPI DISAPPOINTS BUT SEEN AT PEAK.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN APRIL CPI DISAPPOINTS BUT SEEN AT PEAK.

text.p: South Africa's annual consumer price inflation, kicked higher by increased medical costs, came in at a worse-than-expected 9.9 percent in April but economists said the the rate should now have peaked.
The bond market took the figure, which compared to the Reuters consensus of 9.6 percent, in its stride. Dealers said there was some relief that inflation had at least held below the 10 pecent mark.

"I think we're in a period now where for most of the rest of this year it's going to hover between the nine and 10 pct level. It's probably the top but it's not going to subside as quickly as some observers think," said Nick Barnardt of BOE NatWest.

Anastasia Gekis of ABN Amro said the data was disappointing, especially since the market was looking to the April figure to provide a basis for a trend decline for the rest of the year. But she remained confident that the inflation rate should fall from now on.
"It also puts a bit of a damper on hopes for an interest rate cut. It probably delays it slightly, to near the end of the year," she said.
But a bigger consideration for Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals would be the release of April money supply and private credit extension data, expected at 1500 GMT, analysts said.
The Central Statistical Service said the year-on-year CPI rise of 9.9 percent versus March's 9.6 percent was the highest rate since the 10.0 percent recorded in June 1995.
The month-on-month rate of increase was 0.9 percent against 0.6 percent in March.
Medical care and health expenses contributed 0.3 percentage point to that monthly rise, mainly due to the annual increase in the membership fees of medical schemes.
Tony Twine, senior economist at Econometrix consultancy, said the underlying picture for inflation was not too bad, stripping out medical costs.
"The movements of the various components were reasonably under control with the major exception of medical costs where there is a once a year affect in April," he said.
"I don't think it has a lot (of interest rate implications). The one-off nature of that medical adjustment will be recognised as not a permanent contribution to rising prices by the Reserve Bank."
